schools.summary: Gill leans to the informers acting on their own account, out of fear of what David would remember on coming to the throne, and keeps the use of means alongside trust in protection.
Henry inclines to an under-hand hint from the court, and reads David's staying put as a greater valour than resistance would have been.
Clarke explains the three thousand as a calculation against an able general with six hundred men, picked so that the king could depend on them.

Keil and Delitzsch date the second betrayal after the marriage with Abigail; Ellicott takes the three thousand for the standing Gibeah force and raises the question whether this chapter doubles the twenty-fourth.

debates.question: Did Saul set the Ziphites on, or did they act of themselves?

sides.position: Of themselves, in all probability, having already tried to betray David once
Very possibly on an under-hand intimation from Saul; and if not, they were officious men who knew what would please him

outliers.note: Alone in asking why the compiler inserted this chapter at all, and in admitting that no satisfactory answer can be given.

themes: doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah
three thousand chosen men of Israel
David abode in the wilderness
Saul was come in very deed
1.pericope_label: The Ziphites came unto Saul; Saul went down to the wilderness of Ziph

schools.summary: Gill corrects Josephus on the number of companions, grounds the raid in the Spirit of God rather than courage, and makes the object a second proof of innocence.
Henry gathers the chapter's largest thought from the sleeping camp, that sleep given as rest to God's beloved can be made a prison to his enemies.

Clarke works the word for the trench through Luther and Arab camp practice, and notices that the offer repeats what David's men had said at En-gedi; Wesley makes the raid a special instinct with assurance of preservation.
Ellicott settles for the barricade of baggage wagons, and takes the two names as the occasion for excursuses on the Hittites and on the blood feud with Abner.

debates.question: What moved David to enter the camp?

sides.position: Natural courage, an extraordinary impression, or the oracle: it cannot be told, but he went as Gideon did, on assurance of protection
Not courage but the Spirit of God, so that there might be a second occasion of convincing the king
A special instinct, perhaps with foreknowledge of the sleep that had fallen on the camp

outliers.note: Alone in reporting that the Arabs still encamp in a circle with their principal officers in the centre, which he offers as the sense of the disputed word for the trench.

themes: Saul lay in the trench
who will go down with me to Saul
God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand
I will not smite him the second time
5.pericope_label: David and Abishai came to the people by night; let me smite him, I pray thee

schools.summary: Gill keeps to the abhorrence with which the order was given, and is interested in who carried off the spear rather than in what it meant.

Clarke counts the three ways a man finishes his day, holds murder unlawful as taking the matter out of God's hand, and answers the regalia reading with ordinary camp practice; Wesley reasons as a subject about a tyrant who is still lord and king.

Ellicott grounds the inviolability in the anointing, quotes Ewald on the king's ewer and on symbols of royalty received as if in sport, and doubts that a special miracle need be supposed; Keil and Delitzsch take the sleep as sent from the Lord.

debates.question: Was the deep sleep a miracle?

sides.position: A deep sleep sent from the Lord
The word is the one used of the sleep God caused to fall on Adam
No special miracle need be supposed: a friendly district, no fear of surprise, men possibly drinking, and two practised scouts

outliers.note: Alone in reporting Ewald's parallel that a founder of a dynasty is often shown receiving some symbol of royalty by accident or in sport, as Alexander takes the royal divining cup.

themes: destroy him not
the LORD shall smite him
the spear that is at his bolster, and the cruse of water
a deep sleep from the LORD was fallen upon them
9.pericope_label: Who can stretch forth his hand against the anointed of the LORD, and be guiltless?

schools.summary: Gill crosses the valley with Josephus, calls the neglect a great fault if no watch was set, and notes that the rebuke says less than it means.
Henry's note runs through the whole exchange: the general is a man in office bound to inspect the soldiery, who lost his honour and deserved to lose his head.
Clarke reads the address as a strong irony and still acquits the guards, whose neglect was the effect of a supernatural sleep; Wesley keeps to the carrying power of a voice in the night air.

Keil and Delitzsch make the distance a mark of accurate tradition and of David's reduced trust, and hold that the reproaches were aimed past Abner at the king; Ellicott defends valiant for the Hebrew word and hears a deadly feud in the sarcasm.

sides.position: Guilty of a great fault if the watch was never set, that being the general's business
Worthy to die by martial law, the general being unworthy of his office
Not to blame at all, their neglect being the effect of a supernatural sleep

outliers.note: Alone in drawing the rule that those who unjustly condemn others are sometimes justly left to fall into condemnation themselves.

themes: David stood on the top of an hill afar off
answerest thou not, Abner?
wherefore hast thou not kept thy lord the king?
see where the king's spear is
13.pericope_label: David cried to Abner: wherefore hast thou not kept thy lord the king?

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the general's ignorance of the voice from the king's recognition, and reads the plea for his blood both as a warning and, on another rendering, as a confidence.

Clarke offers two senses for the offering, makes the exile a sentence to idolatry, and ends with Harmer's account of hunting partridges to exhaustion; Wesley makes the sacrifice a joint one and the warning plain.
Ellicott weighs Wordsworth's smoother rendering against the plain literal sense, faces the question whether God sets a man on to do evil, and prefers far from the presence of the LORD.

debates.question: What is meant by letting the LORD accept an offering?

sides.position: Either that God take David's life at the king's hand as a sacrifice, or that he accept the king's thanks for purging the land
That David be told his offence and bring a sacrifice for it, following Wordsworth and the Targum
That the king pray the temptation away, which most scholars take as the plain sense
That both men join in a sacrifice to turn away a wrath lying on both

outliers.note: Alone in making the dread of dying far from the land the LORD loves the thought that governed David's later life and set him on bringing up the Ark.

themes: is this thy voice, my son David?

go, serve other gods
to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge
17.pericope_label: Wherefore doth my lord pursue after his servant? to seek a flea

schools.summary: Gill doubts the repentance as a conscience-forced confession like Pharaoh's, and explains why the spear was sent back rather than kept.
Henry reads a double fault, against God's law and against the king's own interest, and holds that neither confession nor promise came from a principle of true repentance.

Clarke would soften the verb to I have erred, finds a vast dignity in a speech that neither begs nor argues, and prefers the Chaldee reading of the blessing; Wesley alone takes the repentance at face value.
Keil and Delitzsch call it a good intention never carried out and defend the closing words against Thenius; Ellicott hears a ring of falseness and closes with the two anointed kings parting for ever.

sides.position: Meant in the mood he was then in, but not from a principle of true repentance
Forced from a guilty conscience, as Pharaoh's was, without real sense of sin
A good intention never carried out, with no genuine goodwill even in the blessing
Genuine: God touched his heart, and he never attempted the pursuit again

outliers.note: Alone in observing that not one of the officers spoke a word for their master, since they could see which of the two men was under God's keeping.
